sources.locator: C++ Core Guidelines; living guidelines accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to RAII and deterministic cleanup
sources.claim: RAII binds resource ownership to object lifetime: construction acquires or establishes ownership and deterministic destruction releases it during every normal scope exit and stack unwind.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **RAII** (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation) ties a resource to an object's lifetime: the **constructor acquires** it and the **destructor releases** it. Because C++ destroys local objects **whenever a scope ends**, by normal exit, `return`, `break` **or an exception**, cleanup can't be forgotten. It applies to **every** resource, not just memory: `std::ifstream` closes files, `std::lock_guard` unlocks mutexes, `std::unique_ptr` deletes objects, `std::vector` frees its buffer. If you catch yourself writing `close()`, `unlock()` or `delete` by hand on each path, wrap the resource in an RAII type instead.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner opens a log with `FILE* f = fopen(...)`, then has four early returns and a function that can throw. Two paths forget fclose, and under load the program runs out of file handles. An ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends, including when a later operation throws an exception. In this lesson you'll refactor manual cleanup into an exception-safe RAII design.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Constructors and initialization** (establishing invariants) and **Value, reference and const-reference parameters** (ownership intent).

sections.heading: The rule: acquire in a constructor, release in a destructor
Destructors must not fail loudly

includes: Bind files, memory, locks and other resources to object lifetimes.
Replace manual cleanup on every path with RAII types that clean up during unwinding too.
excludes: Writing full custom resource classes with move support (move lesson).

outcomes: Refactor manual cleanup into an exception-safe RAII design.

examples.title: The file that closes itself
examples.situation: An ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends, including when a later operation throws an exception.
walkthrough: **An ifstream:** read_lines acquires the file by constructing in(path).
**Closes automatically when its scope ends:** the early return on STOP still closes it.
**Including when a later operation throws an exception:** if push_back throws bad_alloc, unwinding will run ~ifstream.
examples.result: No path leaks a file handle, and the code has no close calls at all.

examples.title: The mutex left locked
examples.situation: A function calls m.lock(), then returns early on an error without m.unlock(). Every other thread then waits forever.
walkthrough: Manual unlock was skipped on one path.
Use std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m); at the top.
examples.result: The mutex is released on every exit, including exceptions.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: RAII is only about memory allocated with new and does not apply to files, locks, sockets, or transactions.
misconceptions.correction: RAII works for any resource with a release step: files, locks, sockets, database transactions and more. The destructor performs the release on every exit.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The mutex left locked", which RAII type fixes it?

analogy.example: RAII is like **a hotel key card that deactivates when you check out**. You don't have to remember to hand it in: leaving (end of scope), whether calmly or in a fire drill (exception), always ends access.
usefulFor: fire drills still check you out
limitations: Hotels need a desk; C++ uses destructors.
Every resource type can have its own key card.

steps.explanation: The ifstream acquires the file in its constructor.
A later operation throws before any manual cleanup could run.
The ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends, even on an exception.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing RAII during unwinding. Step 1, Acquire: in is open. The ifstream acquires the file in its constructor. Step 2, Throw: exception is bad_alloc; close() called is no. A later operation throws before any manual cleanup could run. Step 3, Unwind: ~ifstream is ran; file is closed. The ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends, even on an exception.

faded.prompt: For "The file that closes itself", explain how an ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends, including when a later operation throws an exception.
expectedEvidence: Names the example "The file that closes itself": manual fclose was skipped on two paths.
An ifstream closes automatically when its scope ends.
This includes when a later operation throws an exception.
No path leaks a file handle.

nearTransfer.prompt: Rewrite a function that uses fopen/fclose with three early returns into one using std::ifstream, removing every manual close. Test each early-return path.

farTransfer.prompt: Wrap a C-style resource (FILE* or a made-up handle API with open/close functions) in a small RAII class or unique_ptr with a custom deleter. Show with a counter that open and close calls always balance, even when an exception is thrown mid-function.
scaffold: Count opens and closes in globals.
Delete copy operations of your class.

remediation.explanation: Search your code for **close, unlock, delete, free**. Each one is a sign a resource isn't owned by an object yet: wrap it in an RAII type.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The mutex left locked".

recap.summary: To refactor into exception-safe RAII, give every resource an owning object that acquires it in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, rely on scope exit and stack unwinding to run destructors on every path, use standard types like ifstream, unique_ptr, vector and lock_guard, and keep destructors from throwing.
